Problem 789. Classifying climate data: Station A
Knowledge context.
Climate descriptions summarize long-term patterns. In a reasoning problem, explicit thresholds let us classify numerical data without hidden knowledge.
Given facts.

Use this classroom classification: cool if mean temperature <12°C; mild if 12–17°C; warm if >17°C. Dry if annual precipitation <500 mm; wet if ≥500 mm. Data: Station A: T=11°C, P=520 mm; Station B: T=19°C, P=780 mm; Station C: T=15°C, P=550 mm.
Rules.
Apply only the stated thresholds. Temperature and precipitation are separate dimensions, so each station receives two labels.
Task.
Classify Station A. Then identify whether any other station has the same two-label class.
Step-by-step solution.
1. Compare T=11 with the temperature thresholds: it is cool. 2. Compare P=520 with 500 mm: it is wet. 3. Compare the combined label with the other stations; matches: none.
Answer.
Station A is cool and wet; no other station has the same class.
Knowledge takeaway.
Classification is the application of clear predicates to data; the rule must be stated before the label is inferred.
Formal model.
Numeric predicates with thresholds; output the conjunction of the temperature and precipitation categories.

G9. Exchange, routes, and capacities
Problem 791. Bottlenecks in the Willow–Northfield exchange network
Knowledge context.
Trade and transport networks have capacities. A single narrow connection can limit a much larger network.
Given facts.

Goods move from Willow to Northfield along two branches: Willow→Iris capacity 7, Iris→Northfield capacity 6; Willow→Oak capacity 2, Oak→Northfield capacity 8. The final warehouse at Northfield can accept at most 10 units.
Rules.
A branch cannot carry more than its smallest edge capacity. Independent branch capacities can be added, but a shared destination capacity can cap the total.
Task.
What is the maximum number of units that can reach Northfield in one period? Identify the bottleneck(s).
Step-by-step solution.
1. Branch 1 is limited by min(7,6)=6. 2. Branch 2 is limited by min(2,8)=2. 3. Together the branches could carry 8 units. 4. The destination accepts at most 10, so the final maximum is min(8,10)=8.
Answer.
8 units.
Knowledge takeaway.
A bottleneck is a local limit that constrains the total possible flow.
Formal model.
Flow network; branch capacity is a minimum along a path; total is the sum of independent branches subject to shared caps.
